Paired frozen-score inference for conditional ratios

Source: vignettes/conditional-late-inference.Rmd
conditional-late-inference.Rmd

This guide explains the covariance and status fields returned by affine_ratio_dnn() and clate_dnn(). Start with the CLATE workflow for inputs and a complete example. For identification, nuisance-learning conditions and asymptotic inference, see the accompanying paper.

A small paired-signal example 

fit <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = matrix(1:4, ncol = 1), x0 = 0,
  numerator = c(2, 1, 4, 3), denominator = c(1, -1, 2, 1), s = 2
)
fit$components
#>      numerator denominator
#> [1,]         2         0.5
summary(fit)$coefficients
#>          estimate std.error statistic   p.value  conf.low conf.high
#> target_1        4  5.830952 0.6859943 0.4927167 -7.428456  15.42846

The numerator and denominator use the same weights, and their paired covariance enters ratio uncertainty. Dividing the numerator SE by the first stage or discarding the component cross-covariance gives a different calculation. Deletions hold supplied signals and geometry fixed; nuisance models are not refitted.

At each target, observations with exactly equal represented selected-metric distance use the same averaged rank weights for both signals. A deletion reduces that block’s size and redistributes the n-1 table’s mass among its remaining members before forming paired covariance. This preserves numerator/denominator dependence and row-permutation invariance up to numerical precision. The accompanying warning records that inference with persistent distance ties is not established. The weight guide gives a worked deletion example. Old tied saved fits require refitting.

Keep the variance scales distinct

Returned field Meaning
components[, "numerator"] Reduced form for a CLATE fit
components[, "denominator"] First stage for a CLATE fit
component_vcov[[j]] Paired component covariance on the estimator scale
theta_vcov[[j]] Ratio variance on the estimator scale
theta_omega[[j]] neff[j] * theta_vcov[[j]], local-limit covariance estimate
se[j] Square root of the ratio variance
neff[j] Inverse sum of squared reporting weights

theta_vcov already includes the local sample-size scaling. Do not divide it by neff again. Covariance lists are marginal across reporting targets; they do not supply covariance between different targets or simultaneous confidence bands.

summary(fit)
#>   localization: s = 2, s/n = 0.5
#> Components: numerator = numerator; denominator = denominator
#> Ratio statuses: ok=1
#>          estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#> target_1        4     5.831     0.686  0.4927   -7.428     15.43
confint(fit)
#>           conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -7.428456  15.42846
diagnostics(fit)
#> <rdistnn_diagnostics>
#>   targets: 1
#>   n_eff  : min=2.5714, median=2.5714, max=2.5714
#>   weights: max(top5 share)=1, max(weight)=0.5
#>   dist   : available for 1/1 target(s)
#>   instrument 1 mass: unavailable
#>   instrument 0 mass: unavailable
#>   clipped propensity mass: unavailable
#>   first-stage statistic: 0.577 to 0.577
#>   top-five squared jackknife-contribution share: 1 to 1

Effective sample size describes the final averaged observation-weight concentration. It is not a count of compliers. Physical radius, instrument-arm support, score dispersion and first-stage strength can vary even when neff is the same. The largest centered pseudo-value-square shares attribute fitted variance to deletion indices, including rank changes; they differ from raw weighted score contributions.

Signed signals and unavailable intervals

Augmented treatment signals can be negative even with one-sided compliance; they are not individual compliance indicators. A finite negative aggregate denominator gives a signed ratio, without replacement or trimming.

Inspect these fields before reporting a CLATE result:

Field What to check
ratio_status ok, zero denominator, component overflow or ratio overflow
negative_denominator A finite negative first stage
near_zero_denominator Numerical cancellation; not a calibrated weak-IV test
covariance_status Available, missing, zero-score or numerically failed covariance
wald_available Whether the reported SE supports the computational Wald output

An exactly zero first stage gives an undefined ratio while retaining component estimates and available covariance. Exact zero score variance gives SE zero and unavailable Wald bounds. A finite ratio may also have unavailable uncertainty. These cases stay visible in summaries and plots; inspect the first stage and status rather than interpreting missing bounds as precision.

CLATE generally differs from an average of stratum-specific LATEs or an ordinary residualized-IV coefficient. Use the paper’s estimand definition when choosing the appropriate workflow.

Ratio confidence sets

The experimental ratio_confidence_set() helper uses the paired estimator-scale covariance. It can return bounded intervals, singletons, half-lines, two rays, all real numbers or empty sets. It remains separate from confint(), which reports pointwise Wald intervals.

ratio_confidence_set(fit$components, fit$component_vcov)
#> Paired ratio confidence sets
#>   target 1: two_rays (-Inf, -0.60543] U [1.3053, Inf) (ok)
sets <- ratio_confidence_set(
  rbind(c(2, 1), c(3, 0), c(0, 0)),
  list(diag(c(.5, 0)), diag(2), matrix(0, 2, 2))
)
sets
#> Paired ratio confidence sets
#>   target 1: bounded [0.6141, 3.3859] (ok)
#>   target 2: two_rays (-Inf, -1.1588] U [1.1588, Inf) (ok)
#>   target 3: all_real (-Inf, Inf) (ok)
vapply(sets, function(x) x$type, character(1))
#> [1] "bounded"  "two_rays" "all_real"

Finite endpoints are included. An unresolved result reports a numerical status without asserting a set geometry; it differs from a mathematically empty set. Materially indefinite or unavailable covariance is rejected. At tol = 0, any negative determinant of the represented covariance is rejected, while an exactly singular positive-semidefinite matrix remains admissible. With a positive tolerance, a small negative determinant can instead produce the unresolved near_psd_boundary status. See ?ratio_confidence_set for input validation and returned fields.

Neither a finite Wald interval nor this experimental inversion establishes uniform coverage under weak first stages. The paper describes the scope of its inference results. Numerical safeguards and successful array tests do not establish the statistical assumptions for a particular application.
